candidates.author: G. K. Chesterton
candidates.sourceEdition: The Man Who Was Thursday: A Nightmare, J. W. Arrowsmith, Bristol, with London distribution by Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent & Co., 1908
candidates.notes: Project Gutenberg eBook #1695 is the complete-text candidate and identifies the work as public domain in the USA. The 1908 original scan is identified by Wikimedia Commons as a 340-page file from the Internet Archive, published by J. W. Arrowsmith and Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent & Co.; author death is recorded as 14 June 1936. The Intellectual Property Office of Ireland states literary copyright expires 70 years after the author's death and typographical arrangement of a published edition after 50 years; this supports a preliminary calculation of the underlying text entering the Irish public domain on 1 January 2007 and the 1908 edition layout term expiring after 1958. This is a preliminary source-based calculation, not legal sign-off; edition-specific additions and territorial exceptions still require review. Gutenberg HTML confirms chapter I and the ending marker; sampled chapter headings include I, IV, X and XIV, but a full page-by-page comparison of the Gutenberg text against the original scan remains outstanding. The Wikisource transcription is CC BY-SA and must not be copied into CICAN without meeting its attribution/share-alike terms. A named human transcription reviewer remains outstanding. Do not publish until all gates pass. Additional scan-structure verification (27 Nov 2026): the Wikisource index for the 1908 J. W. Arrowsmith scan reports all pages of the work proper validated and fully transcluded, with validation dated November 2025. The linked scan file is 340 pages; the index exposes the dedication to Edmund Clerihew Bentley and all 15 chapter titles, and its page sequence includes the preliminary roman-numbered matter and printed pages 9–330. This materially strengthens the scan's structural usability as a witness, but the Wikisource validation is not an independent CICAN comparison of Gutenberg against the printed pages. The Wikisource transcription is licensed CC BY-SA; use it only to locate and inspect the scan witness, not as CICAN source text absent licence compliance. Source records: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Index:Chesterton_-_The_Man_Who_Was_Thursday.djvu and https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/File:Chesterton_-_The_Man_Who_Was_Thursday.djvu. A complete independent comparison of Gutenberg #1695 against the scan, including front matter, dedication, all chapter text, punctuation and ending, plus named human review and territorial rights sign-off, remains outstanding. Additional page-level source inspection (27 Nov 2026): the Wikisource index page directly identifies title, author, 1908, publisher J. W. Arrowsmith, London; it lists the dedication and all 15 chapters and marks the work proper fully transcluded/validated. Individual validated page records were opened for the imprint leaf (DjVu page 7: Bristol, J. W. Arrowsmith, 11 Quay Street; London distributor Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent & Company Limited), printed page 9 (DjVu page 13, opening of Chapter I), printed page 58 (DjVu page 62, mid-Chapter III), and printed page 170 (DjVu page 174, mid-narrative). These checks establish accessible page-level scan transcription at multiple points, not a complete collation against Gutenberg #1695. The text shown on Wikisource remains CC BY-SA and is not to be copied into CICAN absent licence compliance. Independent page-by-page comparison, including exact front matter, all chapters, punctuation, and final page, plus named human reviewer and Ireland/US rights sign-off remain outstanding. Further comparison sample (27 Nov 2026): the validated Wikisource scan page for printed page 58 (DjVu page 62) contains the passage beginning 'Comrade Gregory saying to us' and continuing through Syme's speech. Project Gutenberg #1695's official HTML search-indexed text contains the same passage with matching wording and punctuation in the retrieved excerpt. This is one sampled agreement, alongside the previously recorded edition/structure checks; it does not establish full fidelity, because the complete Gutenberg text has not been compared page by page and other sampled pages have not yet been systematically aligned by printed page. The official Gutenberg record identifies eBook #1695, author Chesterton (1874–1936), release 1 April 1999, last update 5 February 2024, and its own US-only public-domain statement. Continue to treat US status as source-declared and Irish status as preliminary pending independent legal review. Sources: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1695 and https://www.gutenberg.org/files/1695/1695-h/1695-h.htm. Additional independent-text lead (27 Nov 2026): the European Literary Text Collection (ELTeC) entry for this work is hosted by TextGrid Repository as edition PID hdl:21.11113/0000-000F-EFA0-F, with a related work record and TEI corpus PID hdl:21.11113/0000-000F-F013-C. TextGrid states the corpus is CC BY 4.0 and cites the edition as TextGrid Repository (2023), Chesterton, Gilbert Keith, The man who was Thursday. The ELTeC English corpus index identifies the record as ENG19080, year 1908, author Chesterton (1874–1936), 57,988 words, quality level high. This is a valuable independently curated, separately licensed comparison text and may be usable with CC BY 4.0 attribution, but the public metadata does not identify the precise printed exemplar or establish that its text is a diplomatic transcription of the 1908 Arrowsmith first edition. The TEI download endpoint was discoverable but the research interface could not render its application/tei+xml content, so internal editorial notes, source statement, and actual text have not yet been inspected. Do not treat it as scan-verified source text or replace Gutenberg with it until its TEI metadata and full content are obtained and aligned against the 1908 scan. Sources: https://www.textgridrep.org/browse/41gjg.0 ; https://distantreading.github.io/ELTeC/eng/index.html ; https://www.textgridrep.org/browse/41gjf.0.

candidates.author: John Buchan
candidates.sourceEdition: The Thirty-Nine Steps, William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London, 1915, first book edition (reported publication date 19 October 1915)
candidates.notes: Project Gutenberg eBook #558 supplies a complete English text candidate and explicitly marks it public domain in the USA; its HTML exposes ten chapter headings and the September 1915 dedication. The National Library of Scotland confirms serialisation in Blackwood's Magazine in July–September 1915 and book publication by William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London, in October 1915. A Google Books record linked from the 'Other editions' list is marked Full view - 1915 and exposes PDF, EPUB and plain-text download controls; its record ID is S0pAO7s-TkEC. The PDF download request returned HTTP 403 through this research interface, so scan pages have not yet been obtained or collated. Ravn Forlag's 2026 edition states its text was read page by page against a Google-digitised scan of the first edition, preserving wording, British spelling, chapter titles and dedication but correcting and documenting obvious misprints; this is useful corroboration, not a reusable transcription because its 2026 editorial contributions are separately protected. A rare-book dealer independently describes a 1915 first edition, William Blackwood and Sons, with pagination [9], 10–253, [3]. John Buchan (1875–1940) supports a preliminary Irish life-plus-70 calculation of 1 January 2011 under IPOI guidance; Gutenberg explicitly marks US public-domain status. These are preliminary source-based findings, not legal sign-off. Exact scan-page acquisition and independent page-by-page comparison of the Gutenberg text, review of any edition-specific elements, and named human transcription review remain outstanding. Do not publish until all gates pass.

candidates.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
candidates.sourceEdition: The Lost World: Being an Account of the Recent Amazing Adventures of Professor George E. Challenger..., Hodder & Stoughton, London, 15 October 1912, first edition in book form
candidates.notes: Project Gutenberg eBook #139 provides a complete English text candidate and explicitly identifies it as public domain in the USA. Google Books identifies a Harvard University digitisation of The Lost World, Hodder & Stoughton, 1912, 309 pages; its contents list all 16 chapters, but this Google Books record currently presents snippet view rather than a page-readable full scan. Open Library identifies a 1912 Hodder & Stoughton edition with 319 pages and eight leaves of plates, linked to Internet Archive item lostworld0000sira_n3v3; other catalogue records identify lostworld01doylgoog and lostworld00doyluoft as 1912 digitised copies, but the exact imprint/issue and image completeness must be confirmed from title-page and collation evidence before using them as the first UK book edition. Peter Harrington's bibliographical catalogue describes the first edition in book form as London, Hodder and Stoughton, [1912], with frontispiece and seven plates; an ABAA catalogue gives 319, [1] imprint pages and plates. Pagination and plate counts differ between catalogue records, so this is not yet a settled edition identification. The novel was serialised in The Strand and Philadelphia Press before book publication; Oxford University Press notes textual variants between serial and first book edition, so Gutenberg must be compared against the exact first book edition, not the serial. Doyle died 7 July 1930; under IPOI life-plus-70 guidance this supports a preliminary Irish public-domain date of 1 January 2001 for the underlying text, while the 1912 typographical arrangement term appears to have expired after 1962. Gutenberg explicitly states US public-domain status. This is a preliminary source-based calculation, not legal sign-off. Any illustrations require separate rights review; text-only is the intended route unless image rights are independently cleared. No page-by-page collation or named human transcription review has been completed. Do not publish until exact-edition collation, Ireland/US rights review and all human attestations pass. Additional high-value scan candidate located: Internet Archive identifier lostworldbeingac00doylrich, digitised by the California Digital Library and mirrored on Wikimedia Commons as a 344-page, 16.07 MB PDF. The scan metadata gives title, author Arthur Conan Doyle (1859–1930), London/New York, Hodder and Stoughton, publication date [1912], and links directly to the IA PDF. This is materially closer to the target first UK edition than the earlier generic Google Books references, but Commons categorises the scan under an unverified-scan category; title-page, edition statement, collation, illustrations and all text pages must be checked before accepting it as the definitive 1912 first-edition witness. The PDF timed out through the web reader and direct download failed in this session; no page-level comparison has been performed. The Google Books Harvard record separately confirms a 1912 Hodder & Stoughton digitisation with 309 catalogue pages, while first-edition bookseller catalogues describe the UK first edition as 319 pages plus imprint and eight illustrations/plates; catalogue pagination differences likely reflect front matter and scanning conventions and must be reconciled, not assumed away. Source-quality clarification from the Commons file record: the PDF is 344 scanned pages (file 16.07 MiB; Commons preview says 7.05 MB), and its bibliographic description names London/New York, Hodder and Stoughton, [1912], OCLC 263174507, and IA identifier lostworldbeingac00doylrich. The Commons structured inception field says 1894, which conflicts with the record's own title, publisher, and 1912 bibliographic sources and appears to be unreliable metadata; do not treat 1894 as the edition date. The scan is hosted under a public-domain label for the US pre-1931 publication rule, but this label does not replace Irish rights analysis. The Oxford edition's note explicitly states the 1912 first book edition replaced some serial illustrations and contains numerous textual variants from the serial, mainly punctuation in the final chapters; it gives three examples of wording/punctuation differences between the Strand text and the first book edition. This reinforces the need to collate against the 1912 book scan. The scan PDF link is recorded, but actual page-level inspection and full comparison remain outstanding. New direct page-level evidence: the Wikimedia Commons scan file The_Lost_World.djvu is linked to Internet Archive item lostworldbeingac00doylrich and contains 344 scanned pages. Its Wikisource index identifies the scan as The Lost World, Arthur Conan Doyle, 1912, Hodder and Stoughton, London/New York/Toronto, and marks all pages of the work proper validated and fully transcluded. The scan's page 7 title leaf itself reads THE LOST WORLD, names Arthur Conan Doyle, and prints HODDER AND STOUGHTON with LONDON NEW YORK TORONTO; that page is marked validated. This is substantially stronger edition identification than metadata alone, but it does not by itself establish the exact first impression or settle the catalogue pagination/plate collation. Wikisource explicitly licenses its transcription text CC BY-SA; CICAN must not copy that transcription without satisfying those terms. The underlying scan images are a distinct source and should be used as the visual collation witness, subject to independent territorial rights review. A human must still compare the complete Gutenberg text against the scanned pages, verify every textual variant and front/back matter, and sign the named review; no such full collation has yet been performed. Sampled collation has now exposed a material difference. The Wikisource scan index identifies the 1912 Hodder and Stoughton volume, marks the work pages validated, and gives the 16-chapter contents; its page 15 (printed page 9), validated, transcribes the opening sentence with British spelling 'centred' and a dash construction. Project Gutenberg #139 gives 'centered' and different punctuation in the same sentence. The scan index contents also gives Chapter XIII as 'A SIGHT WHICH I SHALL NEVER FORGET', whereas Gutenberg #139 gives 'A SIGHT I SHALL NEVER FORGET'. These are concrete sample discrepancies, not a full collation. Wikisource transcription is CC BY-SA and is used here only to locate/check the scan witness; CICAN must derive its own text from appropriately licensed/public-domain scan images, not copy the Wikisource transcription. This confirms Gutenberg #139 is not yet demonstrated to be a faithful transcription of this scan and cannot be accepted as-is. Full page-by-page independent collation, exact issue/impression confirmation, Ireland/US rights review, and named human sign-off remain outstanding. Collation clarification (27 Nov 2026): direct inspection of the validated Wikisource scan page for printed page 9 (DjVu page 15) confirms the first paragraph reads 'centred' and uses a dash after 'earth'; Gutenberg #139 reads 'centered' and uses a comma after 'earth'. The scan page is explicitly marked validated. The scan index's contents page also gives Chapter XIII title 'A SIGHT WHICH I SHALL NEVER FORGET', while Gutenberg's contents gives 'A SIGHT I SHALL NEVER FORGET'. This supersedes the earlier imprecise note that located the opening variant on printed page 15; the verified location is printed page 9. The scan index reports all work pages validated, but validation status applies to the Wikisource transcription and is not an independent CICAN collation. Wikisource page transcription is CC BY-SA; use it only as a reference and do not copy it into CICAN absent licence compliance. Gutenberg #139 is not yet a faithful match to this witness; the full book still needs independent page-by-page comparison and correction from a source CICAN can lawfully use. Exact issue/impression confirmation, territorial legal review and named human sign-off remain outstanding.
